name: git
one_line: distributed version control: track, share and recover changes
plain: `git` records snapshots of a folder (called commits) so you can see what changed, go back to an earlier version, and share work with others. A folder tracked by git is a repository.

The daily loop is: change files, `git add` the ones you want in the next snapshot (the staging area), `git commit` to record it, `git push` to send it to a server such as GitHub, `git pull` to bring others' work down.

For security work git has a second use: repositories leak secrets. An old commit, a deleted file or a hidden .git folder on a web server often holds passwords and keys. This page is focused on the most-used commands and cases, not every option.
when: Get a copy of a project (clone) and keep it up to date.
Save your own work in steps and undo mistakes.
Work on a feature in a branch and merge it.
Search a repository's history for a leaked password or flag.

examples.title: Copy a repository
examples.explain: Downloads the whole project with its history into a folder named project.

examples.title: See what has changed
examples.explain: status lists changed and new files; diff shows the line-by-line changes not yet staged. git diff --staged shows what is staged.

examples.title: Save a snapshot
examples.cmd:
git add notes.md
git commit -m 'Add notes for web labs'
examples.explain: add puts the file in the staging area, commit records it with a message. git add -A stages everything.

examples.title: Send and receive
examples.cmd:
git push origin main
git pull
examples.explain: push uploads your commits to the remote called origin on branch main. pull downloads and merges new ones.

examples.title: Look at history
examples.explain: One line per commit, with branches drawn. -p adds the changes; -n 5 limits the count.

examples.title: Branch and merge
examples.cmd:
git switch -c fix-typo
# edit and commit
git switch main
git merge fix-typo
examples.explain: switch -c creates and enters a branch. After committing there, go back to main and merge it in.

examples.title: Undo carefully
examples.cmd:
git restore notes.md
git restore --staged notes.md
git revert abc1234
examples.explain: restore throws away uncommitted changes in a file; --staged unstages; revert adds a new commit that cancels an old one. These are the safe undo tools.

examples.title: Park unfinished work
examples.explain: stash puts your uncommitted changes aside so you can switch branches; pop brings them back.

examples.title: Hunt for a leaked secret
examples.explain: -S finds commits that added or removed that text. rev-list --all gives every commit to search. Also try git log --all --diff-filter=D --name-only to find deleted files.

examples.title: Recover a hidden .git from a website (lab)
examples.cmd: wget -r http://10.10.10.5/.git/ && cd 10.10.10.5 && git checkout -- . && git log
examples.explain: If a web server exposes /.git/, downloading it gives the whole project and history. Tools such as git-dumper automate this. Only on authorised targets.

examples.title: Ignore files
examples.explain: Names in .gitignore are never added by accident. It does not remove a file that is already tracked.

mistakes: Committing secrets: a password pushed once stays in history even if you delete the file later. Rotate it.
git reset --hard or git checkout -- . throws away uncommitted work with no undo.
Force-pushing (git push --force) over other people's commits.
Working directly on main when a branch would be safer.
Forgetting git pull before starting and getting merge conflicts.
Assuming .gitignore removes files already tracked: use git rm --cached.
